summary.text: Vieta's formulas relate the coefficients of a polynomial to sums and products of its roots.
They provide relations between the roots without having to compute the roots themselves.
They are named after the 16th-century French mathematician François Viète, who derived them for the case of positive roots.

facts.label: Named after
facts.value: François Viète (1540-1603), also called Franciscus Vieta

facts.label: Main benefit
facts.value: Relations between roots without computing them

facts.label: Earlier closeness
facts.value: The 12th-century methods of al-Tusi were very close to Viète's

facts.label: Girard's credit
facts.value: Described as first to understand how coefficients come from the roots

items.prompt: A mathematician wants to say something about how a polynomial's roots relate to each other, but she has not solved for a single root. Is that possible?

options.label: No, every relation needs the roots to be computed first
Yes, but only for polynomials with positive coefficients
No, roots can only be studied one at a time
Yes, the coefficients give relations between the roots directly

items.explain: Vieta's formulas provide relations between the roots without having to compute them.

items.prompt: The coefficients of a polynomial are tied to which combinations of its roots?

Only the number of roots
Only the differences between roots

items.prompt: A historian traces the name of these formulas. Which account fits?

items.prompt: A 12th-century Islamic mathematician, Sharaf al-Din al-Tusi, worked on roots of equations. How did his methods compare with Viète's?

They came after Viète's methods by centuries
